exemplars.name: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
exemplars.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java? When should you use each?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the compiler-enforced contract, can articulate when each type is appropriate, and know how modern Java code trends toward unchecked exceptions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Catching Exception or Throwable as a blanket handler, swallowing exceptions without logging, or using checked exceptions for every failure regardless of whether the caller can recover
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that many modern frameworks (Spring, JPA) and languages (Kotlin, Scala) favor unchecked exceptions to reduce boilerplate. Discuss the 'exception translation' pattern and why you should never swallow exceptions silently.

sections.title: The Exception Hierarchy
sections.content:
Java's exception hierarchy is rooted at `Throwable`, which splits into two branches. **Error** represents JVM-level failures — `OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`, `InternalError` — that applications should almost never catch because they indicate the JVM itself is in a broken state.

**Exception** is the branch your code interacts with, and it further splits based on a simple rule: anything that extends `RuntimeException` is **unchecked** (compiler ignores it), and everything else under `Exception` is **checked** (compiler enforces handling). So `IOException`, `SQLException`, `ParseException` are checked — you must catch or declare them. `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, `IndexOutOfBoundsException` are unchecked — they propagate freely.

This hierarchy was designed with a clear philosophy: checked exceptions for **external, recoverable failures** (I/O, network, database), unchecked exceptions for **programming errors** (bugs in your logic). Whether that philosophy has aged well is debated — most modern frameworks have voted with their code by choosing unchecked.

sections.title: Checked vs Unchecked: Side-by-Side
sections.content:
| Aspect | Checked Exception | Unchecked Exception |
|---|---|---|
| Must declare with `throws` | ✅ Yes — compiler enforces | ❌ No |
| Must catch or propagate | ✅ Yes | ❌ Optional |
| Superclass | `Exception` (not `RuntimeException`) | `RuntimeException` |
| Typical examples | `IOException`, `SQLException`, `ParseException` | `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, `IndexOutOfBoundsException` |
| Caller can recover? | ✅ Usually yes | ⚠️ Often no |
| Used for | External failures (I/O, network, DB) | Programming bugs, invalid state |
| Modern framework preference | ⚠️ Declining | ✅ Dominant (Spring, JPA, etc.) |

sections.title: Exception Translation and Custom Exception Design
Anti-Patterns and Production Best Practices
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Checked = compiler-enforced** — `void read() throws IOException` forces every caller to handle or propagate. Use for recoverable failures: file not found, network timeout, parse error
- **Unchecked = RuntimeException** — `throw new IllegalArgumentException("id must be positive")` propagates freely. Use for programming bugs: null access, bad argument, index out of bounds
- **Modern trend: unchecked-first** — Spring's `DataAccessException`, Hibernate's `HibernateException` are all unchecked. Kotlin and Scala dropped checked exceptions entirely to eliminate boilerplate
- **Never swallow** — `catch (Exception e) {}` is the worst anti-pattern. Always `log.error("context", e)` with the full stack trace. Silent catches hide root causes for days in production
- **Never catch Throwable** in normal code — it swallows `OutOfMemoryError` and `StackOverflowError` which should crash the JVM, not be silently absorbed

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The fundamental difference is **compiler enforcement**. A checked exception — any `Exception` subclass that isn't a `RuntimeException` — forces the caller to either catch it or declare it in a `throws` clause. The compiler won't let you ignore it. An unchecked exception extends `RuntimeException` and has no such requirement — it can bubble up freely.

The design intent maps to **recoverability**. Checked exceptions represent failures a caller can reasonably handle: a file not found, a network timeout, a malformed input. The caller has an action to take — retry, use a fallback, show an error message. Unchecked exceptions represent **programming errors**: a null where a value was required, an illegal argument, an array index out of bounds. These are bugs, not conditions you handle at runtime.

In practice, the industry has shifted heavily toward **unchecked-first**. Spring wraps all data access exceptions in `DataAccessException` (unchecked), JPA/Hibernate does the same, and languages like Kotlin and Scala dropped checked exceptions entirely. The reason is boilerplate: checked exceptions force try/catch or throws through every layer of the call stack, even when intermediate layers have no idea what to do with the exception.

My approach: I use **unchecked exceptions by default** and reserve checked exceptions only when I'm designing an API contract where I genuinely want the caller to handle a specific failure mode.

Two rules I never break: first, **never swallow an exception** — if you catch it, at minimum log the stack trace. I've debugged production issues where a silent `catch (Exception e) {}` hid the root cause for days. Second, **never catch `Throwable`** unless you're writing a top-level error handler — catching `Throwable` swallows `OutOfMemoryError` and `StackOverflowError`, which should crash the process, not be silently absorbed.
